text:
“Well?” she asked when they had returned to the drawing room and were seated facing one another, perplexed.

Outside, summer blazed with its rivers of light, its pyres of splendor; there in the deep drawing room, behind the closed shutters, behind the lowered blinds, a restful coolness breathed.

Then he took one of her hands and slowly, with a kind of stealth, caressed it.

“It is strange,” he said, “but you intimidate me. I have always been rather afraid of you. So often I see a kind of mockery on your lips...”

“Really? How odd!”

“Besides, you are right: you must find me almost grotesque. Men in love are very often ridiculous.”

“And women?” she said.

“Women, I believe, almost never are.”

“What? Grotesque?”

“No, in love.”

“Ah, I could not say... But they certainly confess it more rarely.”

“Tell me,” he resumed warmly, “tell me that you will come often, that you will come every day... I want to see you every day! We are so perfectly safe here...”

“I am thirsty,” she replied.

Rafa brought her an orangeade so cold that it misted the crystal of the carafe; then he drank in turn, from the same glass.

“In other years, by this time, I am already in the country,” Rafa said. “The heat is bad for me. This year, however, it is impossible for me to leave; the thought of no longer seeing you is unbearable to me. But what do you intend to do during the summer?”

“I do not know yet; it does not depend on me.”

“And on whom does it depend?”

“Perhaps on my parents, perhaps...” she added hesitantly, “on my brother.”

“And not on me, in any event?”

“On you? How on you?”

“You once told me, while speaking of other things: ‘My family bores me; perhaps a day will come when I shall be free, entirely free, because I want to sing.’ Do you remember telling me that?”

“Yes, I remember, and I repeat: A day will come, perhaps soon, when I shall be free.”

“There, and thinking of that day, I too have had a dream... but one so beautiful that I do not dare tell you.”

“Dreams...” she joked, “dreams have this virtue: they serve to tell things that are too difficult to say.”

“You are right, Loretta,” he admitted. “Then, a dream. That I should get you a small villa, not too far from Villa Giuliani, a little one, for you alone. A hidden villa, with a beautiful garden, an orchard, a stable. You would be free; no one would know who you were. Sometimes, so as not to remain alone, you would open the gate to me.”

“Ah... and that is the dream?”

“Yes, that is it.”

She reflected for a moment, then said:

“Go on.”

“What do you mean?”

“After the summer...”

“Well, after the summer you may choose whatever you like. In autumn, for example, a lovely journey, a little escape by motorcar, if you wish, even abroad, if you wish... And in winter, your house in the city, a lady companion to preserve appearances, a teacher to teach you singing.”

“And in spring,” she exclaimed, tempted nonetheless, “since the year blossoms again, another is put in Lora’s place, and everything begins again: the same villa, the journey, the house in the city... No, thank you!”

“Another? What are you saying? Have you still not understood that I love you, that I have loved you for long months, more strongly every day? That you can make me obey like a child, and that you alone, you alone, must give me back the peace I no longer have?... Another? That word has no meaning! But think for a moment. Do you believe I do not know what risks I run in making you this proposal? Well, what do I care? I do not want to, I can no longer reflect! No danger frightens me. Only say yes! Ask me for whatever you want, but say yes!”

“I am asking for nothing,” she said, regretting having allowed herself to seem so calculating.

“Then listen, hear me...” And he knelt before her armchair and encircled her with his arms.

“What are you doing? What are you doing?”

“Nothing; I am begging you on my knees. Love me a little; be kind to me for once!”

Thus on his knees, leaning toward her in the ardor of his desire, with passionate eyes and a pleading voice, Rafa was almost handsome, and she looked at him.

“Come, leave me alone...” she said, with a certain annoyance.

He held her tightly around the waist and, bearing down on her a little, covered her dress and her wrists with tiny kisses.

“How many mistresses have you had sit in this armchair?” she asked suddenly.

“How many? None.”

“Oh, come now! I am asking out of curiosity.”

“Perhaps,” he said, “some woman has come here, but I do not remember. They were not mistresses, they were not you. If you do not like it, we shall change houses. I had no love before knowing you. Now you seem the first to me. I love you, I love you in every way; you haunt me and you please me. You are beautiful. You have such an indefinable grace that I suffer when I am near you. Be kind to me, do not laugh!...”

She was indeed laughing, but with a somewhat nervous laugh, and her mouth, her eyes, her hands were no longer so calm.

“No, leave me alone...” she pleaded. “Let me go, please... you are hurting me terribly...”

In the half-light he saw her turn pale; he hid his face in her lap, and with his arms he clasped her knees.

She tried to lift his burning forehead, tried to push away that troublesome mouth, but unable to overcome his strength, in sudden anger she thrust her convulsed fingers into his hair.

Then the struggle was brief: desperately, the girl closed her eyes and let herself be carried away...

But she saw another room, at night, with its windows open over a lake white with moonlight, and the stars close and infinite; another man bent over her, covering her with caresses and kisses. And she saw herself again in that bed, and relived the agony of that vanished hour, and it seemed to her, for an instant, that he had returned, that he was there, on his knees, and was kissing her terribly as he had then, and that his hands were running feverishly, ardently, all over her inflamed body, and a mouth was rising, rising to her lips, full of anguish, fever, voluptuousness, and terror...

A little later, the adjoining room was dark, and from room to room, throughout the silent house, the cry of her lost virginity was suddenly heard.




II


At about five in the afternoon, Beppe Cianella entered the Club and, having ordered an iced drink, sprawled indolently on a leather sofa near the small table where Gigi Saletta, nicknamed Saponetta, and several others were playing poker.
